**There are 567 open VA OIG recommendations in this data. OIG's own dashboard shows 586.** The data is current as of **November 4, 2026**, which is 13 days old, and it isn't flagged as stale.

**Why the two numbers are different:** The dataset was checked against OIG's site on November 4, 2026, and the check passed. Comparing the lists row by row turned up exactly the same 567 recommendations in both. The extra 19 on OIG's dashboard are blank rows on OIG's pages that have no recommendation attached. So 567 is the number of open recommendations you can actually identify, and 586 is the total OIG publishes.

**How old the open items are**

By the year each recommendation was published (567 total):

| Year | Open recommendations | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 369 | 103 |
| 2025 | 118 | 47 |
| 2024 | 24 | 14 |
| 2023 | 24 | 8 |
| 2022 | 13 | 7 |
| 2021 | 18 | 9 |
| 2018 | 1 | 1 |

OIG's dashboard groups the same items by age: 409 open less than a year, 160 open 1 to 5 years, and 17 open more than 5 years. Those add up to OIG's total of 586, not 567, because they include the 19 blank rows. Also, the 17 items over 5 years old can't be matched to the dataset's single 2018 recommendation, because the age groups are based on OIG's total and not on these 567 records.

**Things to keep in mind**
- Most open items are recent, but that doesn't by itself mean older problems got fixed. It could also reflect normal closure timing, or changes in how many reports OIG publishes and what it inspects.
- These items are all still open, so they have no closure dates. The data can't tell you how long they'll take to close.
- For scale, the dataset has 15,649 recommendations in total: 14,925 closed and implemented, 157 closed without being implemented, and 567 open.

Sources: [OIG data dashboard](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard) and [OIG recommendations list](https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all). These are totals across all reports, so no single report is the source.

OIG made **148 recommendations** in Healthcare Facility Inspection reports published in 2026, and **80 of them (about 54%) are still open.**

**Data as of 2026-11-04** (13 days old, so not stale). This covers 2026 only up to that date. Any reports published after November 4 aren't included.

| Status | Recommendations |
|---|---|
| Open | 80 |
| Closed, implemented | 68 |
| Closed, not implemented | 0 |
| **Total** | **148** |

**What to keep in mind:**
- **Report counts:** 61 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports were published in 2026, but that number includes reports with no recommendations. The 80 open recommendations come from 31 of those reports.
- **Why so many are open:** All of these reports came out this year, so many of the open items are probably still within normal follow-up time. Being open doesn't mean they're overdue.
- **Fast closures:** The middle (median) time to close for the 68 closed recommendations is 0 days. That means at least half of them were closed the day the report came out, probably because the facility fixed the problem before publication. It isn't a typical time to close.
- **Gap with OIG's own dashboard:** Across all reports, OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages. This affects the overall total, not necessarily the 2026 numbers above.
- **Comparing years:** If you compare these numbers with other years, a change can mean the problems improved or got worse. It can also mean inspection methods, the number of reports, or OIG's focus changed.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's public recommendations listing (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all). I can break down the 80 open recommendations by report, state, or topic, with report numbers and links.

**OIG issued the most recommendations in 2015: 1,914**, spread across 396 reports published that year. This is based on data as of 2026-11-04, which is 13 days old and not stale.

**Next-highest years:**
- 2014: 1,670
- 2013: 1,394
- 2020: 1,211
- 2017: 1,152

Of the 1,914 recommendations from 2015, 1,903 are closed as implemented, 11 are closed as not implemented and none are still open.

**Limits of these numbers:**
- **Older years look small partly because of the data.** Almost no recommendations appear before 2012, even though OIG published many reports in those years. That more likely reflects what OIG's recommendation records cover than how many recommendations it actually made.
- **The totals are slightly lower than OIG's own.** This data has 15,649 recommendations in all, and OIG's dashboard shows 15,778, a difference of 129. That gap is within the accepted tolerance and is unlikely to change which year comes first, since 2015 leads 2014 by 244.
- **Open counts differ too.** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations and this data has 567. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both. The 19-item difference comes from blank rows on OIG's pages.
- **Changes over time can mean more than one thing.** Fewer recommendations after 2015 could mean problems improved. It could also mean OIG changed its inspection methods, published fewer reports or shifted its focus. These counts can't tell those apart.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's recommendations data: https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all

**No, the data doesn't show suicide prevention growing as an OIG theme.** Reports with a recommendation that mentions suicide fell from 56 in 2024 to 11 in 2025. But that drop mostly reflects a change in how OIG inspects facilities, not a clear change in OIG's focus. The data is as of 2026-11-04, 13 days old, and not flagged as stale.

**The counts**

| Year | Reports with a recommendation mentioning suicide | Those recommendations | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 | 155 | about 36% |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 | 132 | about 8% |

Earlier years for context: 34 reports in 2021, 10 in 2022 and 32 in 2023. So the count has gone up and down rather than moving steadily in one direction. Searching for "suicidal" gave exactly the same results, so the search seems to match both word forms.

**What the counts show**
- How many reports and recommendations actually use the word, in each year's published reports, in this copy of OIG's data.
- The share fell, not just the number. Total reports with recommendations dropped only from 155 to 132, so lower report volume doesn't explain the fall.

**What they can't show**
1. **Whether the problem got better or worse.** A falling count could mean facilities improved, or that OIG changed its inspection method, published fewer reports, or shifted its attention.
2. **The likely main cause: a program change.** In 2024, 55 of the 98 matching recommendations came from OIG's older facility inspection program (comprehensive healthcare inspections), which routinely reviewed suicide prevention. That program has no matching recommendations in 2025. Its replacement, the current Healthcare Facility Inspection program, issued 190 recommendations across 2024–2025, and none use the word suicide. In 2025, the matches came from mental health inspections (9), Vet Center inspections (5), national healthcare reviews (3) and hotline inspections (2). So the 2024-to-2025 comparison mixes two different inspection designs.
3. **How much attention OIG gave the subject.** A keyword search only finds recommendations that use the word. It misses related work worded differently and findings that didn't lead to a recommendation. OIG's own "Suicide Prevention" topic tag tells a similar story: 56 tagged reports in 2024 and 14 in 2025. However, OIG tagged only about a quarter of its reports with a topic, so that count is incomplete.
4. **Whether 2025 is complete.** As of the data date, 6 of the 19 recommendations from 2025 are still open. That doesn't affect the counts, but the follow-up record for 2025 is still unfolding.
5. **Anything about specific facilities.** These are system-wide totals. They don't rate any facility.

**Notes from the data source**
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations; this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both, and the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.
- On target dates: a target date is the facility's own estimate. A closure date seems to record when OIG reviewed the evidence and closed the item, which can be months after the work was done. A late closure doesn't show that a facility missed its commitment.

To get a fairer view of the trend, compare within one program, such as mental health inspections across years. Or read the 2025 matches directly to see whether suicide-related findings now appear under different wording.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. The underlying data is at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

**VBA recommendations take a median of 179 days to close, which is about six months.** The middle half closed in 134 to 312.5 days.

**What the 179 days measures:**
- It counts the days from when OIG published the report to when OIG marked the recommendation closed. It is OIG's closure date, not the date VBA finished the work. OIG appears to close a recommendation after reviewing VBA's evidence, which can come months after the fix. So the number is "time until OIG accepted the fix," and it likely overstates how long VBA took.
- It only counts closed recommendations that have a closure date. VBA has 966 recommendations in total, and 923 are closed. 914 of those have a usable closure date, so the median is based on those 914. About 6% of closed recommendations across OIG, mostly from 2013 to 2016, show no closure date on OIG's site.
- 110 of the 914 closed on the day the report came out, probably because VBA had fixed the problem before publication. They count as zero days and pull the median down a little.
- The 43 open recommendations aren't included. Their median age so far is 161 days. The oldest has been open 1,567 days, and 17 have been open more than a year. If these close late, the true typical time would be somewhat longer than 179 days.
- It doesn't show whether VBA met its own target dates. Under the target_basis rule, a target date is VBA's own estimate, and because OIG's closure can lag the actual work, a late closure doesn't prove VBA missed its commitment.

**Other figures:**
- Of the 923 closed recommendations, 897 were closed as implemented and 26 as not implemented, a not-implemented rate of about 2.8%.
- A recommendation addressed to more than one office counts for each of them. That's why this VBA search also returned a few recommendations shared with Information and Technology (11 recommendations, median 330 days) and the Veterans Health Administration (5, median 71 days). Those groups are too small to compare with VBA and overlap with its total, so they shouldn't be added together.

**Notes on the data:** It is current as of November 4, 2026, which is 13 days old and not stale. It comes from OIG's recommendations page (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all) and covers all reports, so no single report number applies. OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all offices, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check matched the same recommendations; the 19-row gap is blank rows on OIG's pages.

OIG made **two recommendations** in report **25-00193-155**, *Healthcare Facility Inspection of the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas*, published July 16, 2026 ([report page](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system) · [PDF](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-07/vaoig-25-00193-155_final.pdf)).

1. **Environment of care:** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment."
2. **Primary care:** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days."

**The clean and safe environment recommendation (Recommendation 1):**
- **Did the facility concur?** Yes.
- **Target date:** January 29, 2027.
- **Status:** Still open. It was open in both checks, on October 28 and November 4, 2026.

**What the facility said it would do** (quoted from its response):
- Environmental Management Services (EMS) staff inspect and clean all areas at least daily. Restroom cleaning is recorded on logs posted on each restroom door.
- Public restrooms have signs with a phone number to call if a restroom isn't clean enough.
- An EMS technician is assigned to inspect high-traffic public restrooms every business day.
- 24 standard operating procedures for cleaning and disinfection were put in place, including dusting and cleaning exam rooms and restrooms. EMS staff finished training on them on June 2, 2026.
- The Chief of EMS checks cleanliness daily, and the Associate Director checks weekly during environment of care rounds.
- At an all-employee town hall on June 2, 2026, all staff were told their part in keeping the environment clean and safe.

**A note on the source text:** The facility's response in this data also includes passages from the body of the report. Those passages cover other issues OIG found: clean and dirty items stored together, expired respiratory masks, an emergency alert system that only police could reset, and a damaged restroom floor. OIG made no separate recommendation for the first three because the facility showed in December 2025 that it had fixed them. Check the PDF (page 12) for the exact wording of the response.

The data is current as of **November 4, 2026** (13 days old, not stale). One general notice about the dataset: OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, and this data has 567. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both, and the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

**The finding that shows up in the most reports is communication of test results. The VA El Paso Healthcare System is not in that group.** This uses data as of November 4, 2026, which is 13 days old.

**The most common finding: test-result communication workflows**

This finding comes from cluster 260, a group of recommendations with matching or very similar wording. OIG's wording is:

> "The Chief of Staff and Associate Director for Patient Care Services develop workflows that describe how each team member participates in the process to communicate test results, in accordance with Veterans Health Administration Directive 1088(1), Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients."

- **How common:** 21 of the 112 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports in the data (about 19%), with 26 recommendations in total.
- **When:** All were cited in 2026.
- **Status:** 17 of the 26 are still open. None were closed as not implemented.
- **Time to close:** The median is 0 days, but it's based on only 9 closed items. Items closed on the day a report comes out pull a small group's median down to 0, so this doesn't mean the issue is fixed quickly.

A theme can be split across more than one cluster, so this cluster doesn't count every test-result finding. A second cluster (261) has related wording: facility test-result policies and workflows should meet VHA requirements, and staff should check that patients are told their results. It appears in 12 of 112 reports from 2025–2026, with 5 open. Both clusters together point to a bigger theme than either count shows alone. A shared cluster suggests a common issue, but it doesn't prove a common cause.

The next most common findings were:
- Keeping a clean environment to reduce infection risk: 11 reports.
- Stable facility leadership: 9 reports.
- Clean and safe patient care areas: 9 reports.

**El Paso**

El Paso's Healthcare Facility Inspection is report 25-00193-155, published July 16, 2026 (on-site January 14–16, 2025): https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system

It has two recommendations, and neither is in the test-result clusters (260 or 261):
1. "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." This is open, with a target date of January 29, 2027. It's in cluster 270, a separate group on clean and safe environments, which matches the themes of the 3rd and 5th most common clusters above.
2. "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." This is open, with a target date of December 31, 2026. It isn't in any cluster.

El Paso's profile shows no repeat findings (the same templated recommendation cited in more than one of its reports). A repeat would only show that an issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.

This doesn't predict what OIG will cite at El Paso's next inspection. My tools estimate a next window around January 2028: the last inspection's end date plus OIG's stated cycle of about three years. That's only an estimate, because OIG publishes no inspection schedule.

**Data notes**
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.
- A facility's VISN comes mostly from OIG's report tags, which use VA's former numbering. It may not match the five networks VA created on July 15, 2026.
- When a finding has no facility response, it means none was extracted from the report. It doesn't mean the facility failed to respond.

Yes. OIG has cited unsecured medication carts many times. It usually recommends that staff secure carts when they're not in use and that managers monitor compliance. Most of these citations come from facility reviews between 2013 and 2016, and a few are more recent. These are the closest matches I found. It isn't a full list.

**Recommendations about unlocked or unattended medication carts**
- **Battle Creek VAMC, MI**, 15-00606-495 (Aug 2015), closed-implemented. OIG recommended "that employees secure medication carts when not in use and that facility managers monitor compliance." Nurses now check that every drawer is locked after each use, and nurse managers do weekly random checks. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-battle-2
- **West Palm Beach VAMC, FL**, 15-00071-158 (Mar 2015), closed-implemented. In the report OIG noted that "two medication carts were unlocked and unattended" on a community living center unit. The facility retrained staff, and managers now do daily rounds to check that carts are locked. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-west-palm-2 (PDF: https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2015-03/VAOIG-15-00071-158.pdf)
- **San Francisco VA HCS, CA**, 15-00607-483 (Aug 2015), closed-implemented. The carts locked automatically after a set time, but staff were told to lock them by hand rather than rely on that. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-san-4
- **VA Greater Los Angeles HCS, CA**, 16-00101-300 (May 2016), closed-implemented. Covered medication carts and automated dispensing machines. Monitoring continued until compliance stayed at 90% for 3 months. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-va-greater-3
- **Charlie Norwood VAMC, Augusta, GA**, 16-00106-211 (Mar 2016), closed-implemented. Covered unsecured carts along with expired medications and undated multi-dose vials. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-charlie-1
- **VA Palo Alto HCS, CA**, 13-00279-156 (Mar 2013), closed-implemented. OIG recommended that carts be "secured at all times." The facility audited carts monthly on every shift. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-va-palo-2
- **Atlanta VAMC, Decatur, GA**, 13-03653-91 (Mar 2014), closed-implemented. Some cart locks were broken, so carts were kept in a locked medication room until replacements arrived. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-atlanta-va-1
- **Orlando VAMC, FL**, 14-00689-142 (May 2014), closed-implemented. Covered medication and supply carts left in exam rooms. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-orlando-va-0

**Related and more recent**
- **Clarksburg VAMC, WV**, 20-03593-140 (May 2021). This hotline report on the multiple homicides there notes that in 2018, carts on one ward were "unlocked and unattended," and that one code opened medication carts across the whole facility. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/care-and-oversight-deficiencies-related-multiple-homicides
- **VA Northport HCS, NY**, 24-00589-17 (Dec 2024), closed-implemented. This is under OIG's current inspection program. It's about medications and supplies left unsecured in the Emergency Department, not carts in a hallway specifically. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-northport-healthcare
- **Aleda E. Lutz VAMC, Saginaw, MI**, 16-00549-302 (Jul 2017). Carts were broken, and they were kept in locked medication rooms until they could be replaced. https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/clinical-assessment-program-review-aleda-e-lutz

**What the facilities did to fix it:** Most retrained staff on locking carts. Managers or charge nurses then did random or daily checks, often continuing until compliance stayed at 90–100% for about 3 months, and reported results to a nursing or environment-of-care committee. Where locks were broken, facilities kept the carts in locked rooms until they were repaired or replaced.

**Limits of this list:** The search tool returns a ranked list, not a count. It doesn't tell you how often OIG has cited this. The data is current as of 2026-11-04 (13 days old, so not stale). I can count these recommendations by year or check whether a particular facility has had this finding.

Here are two examples of what facilities committed to do after OIG found medication carts unsecured. Both are from OIG's older Combined Assessment Program reviews, and both recommendations are now **closed-implemented**.

**1. Battle Creek VA Medical Center, Michigan: Report 15-00606-495 (published Aug 31, 2015)**
- **OIG recommendation:** "employees secure medication carts when not in use and that facility managers monitor compliance."
- **What the facility committed to:** "Inpatient Mental Health Medication Nurses will check to ensure all drawers are securely locked on the medication cart following each opening of the cart. Nurse Mangers will conduct random checks on each medication cart weekly until 100% compliance has been achieved for a 90 day period."
- Target date: October 31, 2015
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-battle-2

**2. VA Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System, California: Report 16-00101-300 (published May 11, 2016)**
- **Finding:** In 3 of 14 patient care areas, medication carts or automated dispensing machines "were unlocked and unattended."
- **OIG recommendation:** "employees secure medication carts and automated dispensing machines when not in use and that facility managers monitor compliance."
- **What the facility committed to:** Staff would watch for secured carts and dispensing machines during Environment of Care rounds "until 90% compliance is sustained for 3 consecutive months." Results would be "reported monthly to Environment of Care Committee and Nurse Executive Council."
- Target date: June 30, 2016. Closed August 18, 2017.
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-va-greater-3

**What the two plans have in common:** Both pair a change in how staff handle the carts with regular monitoring that continues until the facility meets a set compliance level for a set period. Battle Creek required 100% for 90 days. Los Angeles required 90% for 3 months. Other facilities committed to similar things. For example, the San Francisco VA (report 15-00607-483) told staff not to rely on the carts' automatic timed lock.

**About this data:**
- It is current as of November 4, 2026 and is not stale.
- These two examples come from a ranked search, so they are not a complete list or a count of every time OIG cited unsecured carts.
- Both examples are from 2015–2016 and come from an older inspection program than OIG's current Healthcare Facility Inspection program.

I've put together a prep brief from OIG's public record, current as of **4 November 2026**. That's 13 days old and not considered stale.

## When the next inspection might happen
- **Your last inspection:** the Healthcare Facility Inspection that ended **16 January 2025** and was published **16 July 2026**. Report [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system).
- **Rough estimate for the next one: around January 2028.** This is my tool's guess, not OIG's. **OIG does not publish a schedule.** The tool adds about three years to your last inspection's end date because the program aims for roughly a three-year cycle. OIG doesn't give advance notice, so it's safest to be ready now.

## Your record: 19 reports, 66 recommendations, 4 still open

**1. Clean and safe environment (Environment of Care)**, report 25-00193-155
- **Recommendation:** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." Your target date is 29 January 2027.
- **What you committed to:**
  - Daily inspection and cleaning by Environmental Management Services (EMS)
  - Restroom cleaning logs and signs with a number to call
  - A dedicated EMS technician checking busy restrooms
  - 24 cleaning procedures, with EMS training finished 2 June 2026
  - Daily checks by the EMS chief and weekly rounds by the Associate Director
- **To check before closing it:**
  - Are the logs actually being filled in?
  - Can you show the weekly round results over time?
  - Has the damaged concrete floor in the women's restroom been fixed? OIG noted it's a fall risk and that the VISN's FY2024 workplace evaluation found similar floor damage.

**2. Secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days (Primary Care)**, same report
- **Recommendation:** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." Target date is 31 December 2026, which is about six weeks away.
- **Status:** The procedure for this was still being written when you responded. Monthly reporting to the Clinical Executive Council started 1 June 2026. Your stated goal is zero screenings over 30 days for **six months in a row**.
- **To check:**
  - Is the procedure finished and signed?
  - Do the council minutes show six straight months at zero? June 2026 reporting would reach six months around November or December.

**3–4. Data center physical security**, report [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare), published 27 September 2023
- **Recommendation 5:** a working, monitored video surveillance system for the data center.
- **Recommendation 7:** water detection sensors in the data center.
- Both are assigned to the Office of Information and Technology (OIT), not your facility. The record has no response or target date for either, but the record only captures responses from some reports, so that doesn't mean nothing was submitted or that anything is overdue. These have been open for more than three years, so it's worth asking local OIT where they stand.

**Repeat findings:** none. No recommendation was cited more than once in your reports. This only compares recommendations the tool has placed in a group of similar findings.

## What OIG often cites at other facilities
These are ranked by how often they appear across 112 Healthcare Facility Inspection reports. That isn't a measure of how serious they are, and it doesn't predict what OIG will find at El Paso.

| Theme | How often | Not yet closed |
|---|---|---|
| Written workflows for each service on communicating test results (VHA Directive 1088) | 21 of 112 reports | 17 |
| Test result policy that meets VHA rules, plus tracking whether patients were told their results | 12 of 112 | 5 |
| Clean environment to reduce infection risk (VHA Directive 1608) | 11 of 112 | 11 |
| Stable, consistent leadership (addressed to the VISN Director) | 9 of 112 | 3 |
| Keeping patient care areas clean and safe | 9 of 112 | 2 |

None of your recommendations fall into these five groups. That doesn't mean El Paso was never cited on these themes, because similar findings can sit in other groups. Your open cleanliness finding is close in subject to the two cleaning themes.

**What other facilities committed to:**
- **Test results:** written workflows for each service built from one template, then audited and approved by the Chief of Staff (Madison, [25-00254-277](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-william-s-middleton-memorial)). Training with a 90% target and reports to the Quality and Patient Safety Board (Shreveport, [26-00057-170](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-shreveport-healthcare)). A monthly review of 50 test results until 90% compliance holds for six months (Hampton, [24-00603-86](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-hampton-healthcare-system), closed as implemented). Appendices to the local policy listing services and timeframes for high-risk patients (Harlingen, [25-00189-199](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-texas-valley-coastal-bend), closed as implemented).
- **Cleanliness:** a monthly audit of 20 beds by an EMS supervisor (St. Louis, [24-00600-136](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-st-louis-healthcare-system)). Monthly quality checks looking for dust under exam table mattresses, plus yearly dusting of sprinkler heads (Louisville, [24-03205-235](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare)). An electronic channel for staff to report cleaning problems straight to the Assistant Director (Salisbury, [26-00030-213](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-salisbury-va-health-care)). Monthly rounds by EMS supervisors until 90% compliance holds for three months (Little Rock, [25-00203-180](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-central-arkansas-veterans)).
- **Leadership:** see Augusta ([24-00617-118](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-augusta-health-care-system)) and Boston ([24-00613-162](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-boston-healthcare-system)).

## Suggested next steps
1. **Collect proof for both open 2025 recommendations:** cleaning logs, round records and the restroom floor repair, plus the screening procedure and six months of council reports.
2. **Check that issues OIG accepted fixes for are still fixed.** OIG made no recommendation on these because you'd already acted, but they could come up again:
   - Clean and dirty items kept apart in the primary care and women's health clinics
   - No expired respirator masks in storage
   - Environment of care teams able to get into every room, including locked ones
   - The clinic emergency alarm reset is still in the hallway, not the police station
3. **Ask OIT for an update** on the data center cameras and water sensors.
4. **Review your test result workflows** against VHA Directive 1088, since that's the most common finding at other facilities.

**Caveats from the tool:**
- The groups of similar findings are based on matching wording. They suggest a shared issue but don't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups.
- When a group has only a few closed recommendations, its typical time to close can be misleading. Some show 0 days because items were closed on the day the report came out.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimate, not a measure of missed deadlines.
- The VISN 17 label comes from OIG's tags under the old network numbers and may not match the five networks VA created in July 2026.
- Overall, this data shows 567 open recommendations and OIG's dashboard shows 586. A row-by-row check traced the gap to 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

I can pull the full 2025 report, go through any of your 19 past reports, or list more findings that come up often at other facilities.

**I can't give you that percentage. The public OIG record doesn't support a "missed target date" measure, and any number I gave you would be misleading.**

**Why:** Here is how the data describes target dates: *"A target date is the facility's own estimate. A closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing evidence, which can follow the work by months. A closure after the target, or an open recommendation past it, does not show that a facility missed its commitment."*

In other words, the closure date shows when OIG finished checking the evidence, not when VHA finished the work. Comparing it with the target date would make VHA look late when it may not have been.

**What I can measure: how long VHA recommendations take to close and how many stay open** (data as of 2026-11-04, 13 days old, not stale)

| Measure | VHA |
|---|---|
| Recommendations addressed to VHA | 13,440 |
| Closed, implemented | 12,978 |
| Closed, not implemented | 36 (0.28% of closed) |
| Open | 426 |
| Median time from report to closure | 225 days (middle half: 153 to 326 days; based on 12,164 recommendations) |
| Closed the day the report came out (likely fixed before publication) | 946 |
| Open more than 1 year | 108 |
| Median age of open items | 147 days |
| Oldest open item | 2,078 days (about 5.7 years) |

**Things to know about these numbers:**
- About 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013 to 2016, have no closure date on OIG's site. That's why the 225-day median is based on 12,164 recommendations, not all 13,014 closed ones. Another 11 records had impossible negative closure times and were left out.
- A recommendation addressed to more than one office counts for each. So some VHA recommendations also appear under offices such as OIT or OALC, and the office totals can add up to more than the real total.
- Across all offices, OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations and this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. The underlying records are at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all and https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard.

If you need a true on-time rate, you'd have to ask VA or OIG for the dates when the work was actually finished, which aren't published. I can also break these closure times down by year, report type, or topic.

**OIG doesn't name a "worst" VA medical center, and I can't build that ranking from its records either.**

**Why OIG doesn't rank facilities**
- **Each inspection covers a different scope.** OIG looks at different facilities at different times and checks different areas each time. A facility with more findings may just have had a broader or more recent review.
- **Many reports start with a complaint.** Hotline reports look into specific allegations, so a facility with more of them isn't necessarily worse.
- **Raw counts are misleading.** The number of recommendations depends on the facility's size, how many reports cover it and when they were published. It doesn't measure quality of care.

The data I can search reports what OIG found and what VA did about it. It doesn't score facilities, so I won't rank them.

**What I can look up instead**
- **A specific facility:** what OIG found there, how many recommendations it has, which are still open, and its oldest unresolved item, with report numbers and links.
- **Problems that come up across the country:** for example, issues found again and again in OIG's current Healthcare Facility Inspection program, and how common they are.
- **Comparisons by state or topic:** counts, trends over time, how long recommendations take to close and how many close without being implemented, one state at a time.
- **A specific issue:** findings on topics like suicide prevention, staff credentialing or wait times, and what facilities committed to do.

If you're concerned about a particular VA medical center, tell me which one and I'll pull up its OIG record. If you or someone else needs urgent medical help, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

Nobody can say exactly what OIG will cite at the next inspection, and I won't guess. The public record can show what's still unresolved at El Paso (station 756) and what OIG cites most often at other facilities. Neither one predicts what inspectors will find. The data is current as of **November 4, 2026** (13 days old, not stale).

## When the next inspection might be
- **Last inspection:** Healthcare Facility Inspection, which ended January 16, 2025. The report came out July 16, 2026: [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system).
- **Estimated next window: around January 2028.** This is the tool's guess, not OIG's, and OIG publishes no schedule. The tool added about three years to the last inspection's end date, because OIG says the program runs on a roughly three-year cycle. Reports usually come out months after an inspection, so estimates based on publication dates tend to run late.

## El Paso's 4 open recommendations
These are still unresolved. That doesn't mean OIG will cite them again.

From the 2026 inspection report, [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system):
1. **"Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment."** (Environment of Care; the facility's target date is Jan. 29, 2027.)
   - **Facility's plan:** daily cleaning logs posted in restrooms, an assigned technician who checks busy restrooms, 24 cleaning procedures, staff training finished June 2, 2026, daily oversight by the head of environmental services, and weekly rounds by the Associate Director.
   - **Other items in the same report:** OIG also noted clean and soiled supplies stored together, expired respirator masks, an emergency alarm that only police could reset, and a damaged restroom floor. It made no separate recommendation on the first three because the facility showed fixes in December 2025.
2. **"The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days."** (Primary Care; target date Dec. 31, 2026.)
   - **Status:** The facility says it has no follow-up screenings older than 30 days. It is writing a formal procedure and has reported the numbers monthly to its Clinical Executive Council since June 2026. Its goal is six straight months at zero.

From the 2023 information security inspection, [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare). Both are assigned to VA's Office of Information and Technology:
3. "Ensure a video surveillance system is operational and monitored for the data center."
4. "Ensure water detection sensors are implemented in the data center."

Across 19 reports, El Paso has 66 recommendations in total. The tool found **no repeat findings**, meaning no standard recommendation that appeared in more than one El Paso report. Only recommendations that fall into a group of similar findings get compared, and a repeat would mean an issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.

## What OIG cites most often at other facilities (current inspection program)
These are sorted by how often they appear, not by how serious they are, and they don't predict findings at El Paso:
- **Written steps for how staff share test results with providers and patients:** 21 of 112 reports (for example, [26-00057-170](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-shreveport-healthcare)).
- **Making the facility's test-results policy meet VHA rules and tracking whether patients are told their results:** 12 of 112. Median time to close was 256 days, across 9 closed items (for example, [24-00603-86](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-hampton-healthcare-system)).
- **Keeping the facility clean to reduce infection risk:** 11 of 112 (for example, [26-00030-213](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-salisbury-va-health-care)).
- **Steady, consistent leadership at the facility:** 9 of 112 (for example, [24-00617-118](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-augusta-health-care-system)).
- **Keeping patient care areas clean and safe:** 9 of 112 (for example, [24-00600-136](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-st-louis-healthcare-system)).

None of El Paso's recommendations fall into these groups. That doesn't mean OIG never cited El Paso for these themes, because similar findings can land in other groups. El Paso's cleanliness finding, for instance, sits in a separate group.

## Notes on the data
- Similar findings from other facilities were matched by wording and meaning, so some may not fit their group exactly. A group points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimate and don't measure missed deadlines.
- A recommendation with no facility response just means none was pulled from the report. It doesn't show the facility failed to respond or that anything is overdue.
- The VISN label (17) comes from OIG's tags in VA's old numbering. It may not match El Paso's network under the five networks VA created on July 15, 2026.

If you're preparing for the inspection, I can pull either report in full or look at how other facilities fixed a particular finding.
